analysis.one_liner: Phases lead out of paint, solder, food cans, and gasoline, and sets up battery recycling and lead-poisoning prevention programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in July 1990 with one cosponsor, it got a single subcommittee hearing in September 1990 and died when the Congress ended without any House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred making or selling a long list of products with more than tiny amounts of lead — including paint, solder, plumbing fittings, toys, food cans, and wine-bottle foils. It would have forced smelters and battery plants to monitor and report their lead emissions, required stores to take back used lead-acid batteries for recycling, labeled lead-containing products, and funded testing, abatement training, blood-lead screening, and stricter lead standards for air and drinking water. It never got a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and residents of older housing, who bear the brunt of lead poisoning from paint, dust, soil, and water; households drinking tap water in homes with lead plumbing or lead-soldered pipes; communities near lead smelters and battery plants; and consumers who would gain clearer lead labeling and free battery take-back. The bill's own findings state that lead poisoning is the most prevalent environmentally caused disease among American children, with permanent neurologic impairment at common exposure levels [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and residents of older housing

how_it_helps.text: Bans manufacturing and sale of paint, solder, plastic additives, plumbing fittings, toys, fishing weights, and other products above strict lead-content limits, cutting new lead released into homes and the environment [S2] [S3].
Bans lead-soldered food cans within 18 months and stops leaded gasoline from being priced below unleaded, removing two major dietary and airborne lead sources [S2] [S3].
Requires lead smelters, refiners, and battery plants to install emissions monitors and report releases to air, water, and land, with the data published in the Federal Register [S2] [S3].

Creates a nationwide lead-acid battery recycling system: retailers, wholesalers, and manufacturers must accept used batteries at no charge, and discarding them any other way becomes illegal [S2] [S3].

Funds lab certification, worker training for lead-paint abatement, public education, university research centers, a blood-lead laboratory reference project, and sets firm deadlines for stricter national air and drinking-water lead standards, including a 5-microgram-per-liter tap-level drinking water limit if EPA fails to act within a year [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, processors, importers, and sellers of lead-containing products: paint, solder, can, plumbing, and battery makers would bear reformulation, monitoring, reporting, labeling, and take-back costs; lead smelters would face emissions monitoring; and battery retailers would absorb collection duties, with costs likely passed partly to consumers. Federal spending of roughly $95 million over four years is authorized [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Reformulating paint, solder, cans, and other products imposes real compliance costs on manufacturers, some of which would reach consumers in prices; the bill itself acknowledges this by letting the EPA raise a limit for three years where no comparable substitute exists [S3].

The battery take-back scheme shifts collection logistics and costs onto retailers and wholesalers, and prohibits charging customers fees for accepting used batteries, which small sellers would have to absorb [S3].

The bill authorizes roughly $95 million in new federal spending over fiscal years 1991-1994 and layers a new EPA program, coordinator, and research centers on top of existing environmental and health authorities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case was strong: lead causes permanent neurologic damage in children, and the bill targeted the main continuing sources — paint, solder, cans, gasoline pricing, smelter emissions, and discarded batteries — while also funding the testing and abatement capacity needed to deal with lead already in older housing. The costs fall mainly on identifiable industries and partly on consumers, and a few niche products (like stained glass) had no ready substitutes, though the bill allowed EPA case-by-case relief. On balance the benefit to children's health and drinking-water safety clearly outweighed the compliance costs, though the program's design was ambitious and expensive for its time.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never reported it out; it spent its whole life in two subcommittees, got one hearing, and expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas A. Luken of Ohio, joined by Rep. Sikorski, introduced the Lead Pollution Prevention Act of 1990 on July 25, 1990 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction [S5].
On August 31, 1990 it was sent to two subcommittees — Transportation and Hazardous Materials, and Health and the Environment [S5].
The subcommittees held a hearing on September 19, 1990, but the full committee never took action and the bill never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers, processors, and sellers of lead-containing products — paint and solder makers, food-can manufacturers, lead smelters, and battery manufacturers and retailers — are better off because the bill died: they avoided lead-content bans, emissions monitoring and reporting, labeling rules, and mandatory no-fee battery take-back. Nothing in the record shows a committee report, floor vote, or companion Senate action [S5] [S1].

for.name: Rep. Thomas A. Luken
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to a subcommittee hearing.

for.name: Rep. Gerry Sikorski
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's original cosponsor at introduction; the bill drew only one additional Democratic cosponsor afterward.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup after referring it to two subcommittees.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had only a single Democratic cosponsor, so the record shows too little support to tell whether the inaction was partisan or simply reflected thin interest.

industries.note: Primary and secondary lead smelters and refiners would have had to install emissions monitors and report releases to air, water, and land annually, with data published. Their interest ran against the public's interest in knowing and limiting lead emissions.

industries.industry: Lead-acid battery manufacturers, wholesalers, and retailers
industries.note: They would have been required to accept used batteries from customers at no charge, arrange retailer pickups, and post consumer notices, with penalties for violations. The costs of the take-back system would fall on the industry, while improper battery disposal — a major lead source — was the target.

industries.industry: Paint, solder, plastics, and construction-products makers
industries.note: The bill banned manufacture of paint, solder, plastic additives, plumbing fittings, and building materials above strict lead limits one year after enactment, forcing reformulation. Lead in these products was a chief cause of childhood lead poisoning.

Lead-soldered food cans would have been barred from manufacture within six months and sale within eighteen. Lead solder in cans put lead in the food supply, so the industry's cost was the public's gain.
The bill barred offering leaded gasoline below the price of unleaded at the same station, removing a price incentive that steered drivers to the more polluting fuel.
